hero.method: Transparent keyword rule over the regulator's verbatim hazard sentence. Matched terms are recorded per row so the classification is auditable. See hazard_class().

survival_curve.method: isotonic regression (PAVA), nonparametric MLE for current-status data
survival_curve.assumption: survival is monotone non-increasing in days since recall
survival_curve.confound: Age is confounded with cohort: a 2024 recall is not exchangeable with a 2026 one. This is a cross-sectional age profile, not a within-product survival trajectory.
survival_curve.interval_method: Wilson score interval on the isotonic block supporting each grid point. A percentile bootstrap is deliberately NOT used: it is known to be inconsistent for Grenander-type monotone estimators at a fixed point, and on this corpus it returned intervals that excluded their own point estimate. These intervals condition on the fitted block structure, so they describe uncertainty in the level within a block, not uncertainty in where the block boundaries fall.

hunt._what: A manual hunt, outside the three collector arms. NOT sweep results.
hunt._why_separate: Every row here was fetched by hand with `bdata scrape`, one URL at a time, from markets no collector covers. They are not adjudicated sweep output, they do not appear in `rows`, and they do not touch `survival`, `border_escape` or any arm. Mixing a hand-found row into a collector result would be the single most dishonest thing this project could do, so the two are kept in different files and rendered in different sections.
hunt._why_it_exists: The three arms adjudicated every listing they returned, across 207 notices, and reached zero RED. That is either an absence or a blind spot, and the two look identical from inside the sweep. This is the test that separates them: search markets the arms never covered, by hand, and see whether the products are there.
hunt._method: bdata scrape <url> --format markdown, then the fetched page text run through collector/normalize.py classify(), the same adjudicator the sweep uses. No rule was relaxed. Verdicts below are the code's.
hunt._result: One RED, adjudicated by the sweep's own classifier over a committed page. A second row the classifier also called RED, held down to AMBER by hand because the recall is scoped to a date code the listing cannot show. Two further live listings at AMBER. The zero was a coverage artifact, not an absence.

hunt.what_this_establishes: The three collector arms cover amazon.com, kaufland.de and flipkart.com. They adjudicated every listing they returned and confirmed nothing. One afternoon of hand searching, in markets those arms do not cover, found a recalled scooter on sale, a recalled child car seat base on sale, and two more live listings with stated caveats. The sweep's zero is therefore a statement about where we looked, not about what exists.
hunt.what_this_does_not_establish: Nothing here changes the sweep. Survival remains 0 of 180 with its interval, because that figure describes the three arms and these rows are not from the three arms. A hand-found row has weaker provenance than an adjudicated one: it was chosen by a human who was looking for it, so it carries selection bias a systematic sweep does not, and it cannot be used to estimate any rate.
hunt.the_honest_sentence: We looked in three marketplaces and found nothing. We looked in a fourth and found it in an afternoon. The distance between those two sentences is the whole problem with checking whether recalls work.
hunt._provenance: Every fetched_at below is the modification time of the committed artifact holding that fetch, not a time typed from memory. The raw pages are in data/hunt/ so any verdict here can be re-derived by running collector/normalize.py classify() over them without re-fetching.
hunt._verdict_fields: code_verdict is what collector/normalize.py classify() returns when run over the committed page, re-derived by data/hunt/rederive.py on every run. published_verdict is what we are willing to assert. They differ on CPSC 24346 only, where the code says RED and we publish AMBER. The downgrade is conservative and is shown on the wall.

platform_jobs._what: Bright Data's OWN telemetry about our collections, recorded where it disagrees with our health board.
platform_jobs._why_this_file_exists: Our health board computes `fails` from what the collector returned to us. That is self-reported health, and self-reported health cannot see a page that never reached us. On 2026-08-20 the platform's monitoring flagged a 20% page failure on a US collection while our own board recorded fails: 0 for the US arm on that day. Neither number is wrong. They measure different things, and the distance between them is a real limitation of every health board that only reads its own output. This project exists to refuse clean screens over broken scrapers, so the honest move is to publish both numbers and name the gap, not to quietly adopt theirs or ignore it.
platform_jobs._provenance: Transcribed from a Bright Data 'Low success rate' alert email, subject line "Low success rate for canon-us", received 2026-08-21. It is operator-supplied evidence, not an API read: we do not currently poll the platform for job telemetry, which is itself the finding. Nothing here is inferred and nothing is rounded.
platform_jobs._limitation: This is ONE job. It is not a success rate for the sweep, for the US arm, or for any other collection, and it must never be presented as one. Eight pages is a small run and 2 failures out of 8 carries an interval far too wide to characterise anything.
